To sell books… on the internet. In the 90s. People thought it was a joke. Jeff Bezos wasn’t building for approval. He was building for the future. For years, Amazon made little to no profit. Investors doubted. Critics laughed. The market misunderstood. But he stayed obsessed. Because he understood something most people don’t: If you need validation early… You will quit before it works. Amazon didn’t win because it was obvious. It won because it survived long enough to become undeniable. This is the truth: If you cannot endure being misunderstood… You cannot build anything great. If you see yourself in the first list — my DMs are open. #AmazonInvesting #AmazonWholesale #IdealClient #EcommerceBusiness 3 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in Priya Chanduraj 4K followers 1w Report this post Jeff Bezos had a simple rule at Amazon: if a team can't be fed with two pizzas, it's too big. On the surface, it sounds too unrealistic to maintain, but there's real logic behind it. Small teams move faster because there are fewer people to align, fewer opinions to reconcile, and fewer layers standing between an idea and its execution. Ownership is clearer because there's nowhere to hide, and bureaucracy struggles to take root when the team is small enough to sit around a single table. As Amazon grew into one of the most complex organizations on the planet, Bezos was obsessed with one thing: making sure that scale didn't kill speed. The Two-Pizza Rule was one of his answers to that problem. You must keep teams autonomous, accountable, and small enough to get things done. Most companies respond to growth by adding more people to every problem. Amazon responded by drawing tighter boundaries around smaller groups and giving them real ownership over outcomes. As your team or company grows, are you building structures that enable speed or ones that quietly slow everything down? #Finance #Amazon #TwoPizzaRule #Teams 13 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in AJ J Golden Eagle Services•1K followers 1mo Report this post Jeff Bezos built Amazon by designing strategy around reality, not wishful thinking. In the early years, Amazon faced brutal constraints: limited capital, fragile infrastructure, thin margins, unreliable logistics, and relentless pressure from investors who doubted the company would survive. There was no room for ideal conditions or perfect timing. Every decision had to work inside the world as it actually existed. Instead of fighting those limits, Bezos used them as inputs. He prioritized long-term efficiency over short-term profits, invested heavily in customer experience even when it hurt earnings, and built scalable systems that could compound over decades. While others optimized for quarterly results, Bezos optimized for endurance. That mindset shaped Amazon’s operating culture. Progress didn’t come from waiting for better conditions. It came from adapting faster than competitors and turning constraints into competitive advantages. Amazon wasn’t built on optimism. It was built on execution inside hard reality.✨ 18 Like Comment Share Copy LinkedIn Facebook X To view or add a comment, sign in Business Insider 10,940,459 followers 6d Report this post Tiny teams, a flatter workforce, and squiggly lines. Andy Jassy's latest letter to Amazon's shareholders offers fresh insights into how he's thinking about the company's workforce of 1.5 million people globally, including roughly 350,000 corporate hires. The Amazon CEO's missive arrives at a critical point for the company. While its stock is up 26% over the past 12 months, it's virtually flat year to date, and trades 10% below the all-time high it reached in November. His letter championed tiny teams, trumpeted the company's flatter structure, and underlined the need for workers to navigate ambiguity. Stock down 90%. Layoffs. Bankruptcy looming. Instead of playing safe… he did the opposite. He opened Amazon’s platform to competitors. Critics called it business suicide. But Bezos saw what others didn’t: 👉 The future isn’t about owning inventory. 👉 It’s about owning the customer. That one bold decision changed everything. Today, over 50% of Amazon’s sales come from third-party sellers. Lesson: When things fall apart, average players protect. REVEAL: Amazon did not begin with venture capital or a genius business plan executed in isolation. It began with MacKenzie saying yes when the evidence said no. Moving across the country.
